h1: SEO for Ayurveda brands under the AYUSH and DMR rules
metaTitle: SEO for Ayurvedic Brands: AYUSH-Safe Ranking
metaDescription: SEO for ayurvedic brands in India. We publish dosha, herb and therapy content that ranks without breaching AYUSH or Drugs and Magic Remedies rules.
answer: Ayurvedic brands lose more search traffic to Indian law than to Google. The Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954 bans advertising a remedy as a cure for a long schedule of conditions — diabetes, obesity, cancer among them. So rank on herbs, doshas, therapies and named practitioner authority instead.
takeaways: The **DMR Act, 1954** plus Schedule J of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules together list the conditions no remedy may be advertised as preventing or curing. That list is where most ayurvedic landing-page copy lives.

Rule 170 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules — the Ayush advertising approval number — has been notified, un-enforced, proposed for omission and litigated. Treat its status as live, not settled, and build content that survives either way.
Three clusters carry the category: **herb monographs**, **dosha and prakriti content**, and **therapy explainers**. They interlink naturally, which is exactly what topical authority is built from.

A BAMS-qualified author with a registration number is worth more than 50 blog posts. Classical citation plus honest labelling of what modern evidence does and doesn't say is the format that survives core updates.
Export demand is real, and it moves you into someone else's rulebook — DSHEA in the US, Regulation 1924/2006 in the EU. Your Indian copy will not translate legally.

sections.h2: The conditions you legally cannot advertise against
body: Start here, because everything else on an ayurvedic site is downstream of it. The Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954 makes it an offence to advertise a remedy as curing, treating or preventing the diseases listed in its schedule and rules. Rule 106 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules separately points at Schedule J, naming conditions no drug may purport to prevent or cure. Between them: diabetes, obesity, cancer, hypertension, sexual impotence, hair loss and dozens more — roughly an inventory of the category's highest-converting search terms.

The penalties aren't theoretical — a first conviction can carry imprisonment of up to six months, a fine, or both. In practice the commoner outcome is a misleading-advertisement complaint, a state licensing notice, or a marketplace pulling the listing. None of those appear in your analytics as a Google problem. All of them end the traffic.

table.caption: The same query, answered two ways — one of them survives.
head: The page that gets pulled
The page that ranks
Why the second one wins
rows: "What Ayurveda says about blood-sugar management, and what the evidence on each herb shows"
The first is a scheduled condition and a prohibited claim. The second answers what was typed, with sources.
"Bhringraj and amla: traditional use, what small trials looked at, what nobody has tested"
A guaranteed outcome is legal exposure and the exact overclaim Google's raters flag on health pages.
"What happens in each of the five procedures, who they suit, what the preparation week involves"
"Detox" has no agreed clinical meaning. Procedure detail is what people want and nobody publishes.
"Contraindications, interactions, who should not take this"
Absolute safety claims are indefensible for anything pharmacologically active.

body: Rule 170 requires Ayush drug manufacturers to obtain a unique identification number from the state licensing authority before advertising, and prohibits misleading Ayush advertisements. Enforcement has gone back and forth — advisories not to act on it, a proposal to omit it, Supreme Court proceedings that pushed it back up the agenda. Anyone stating flatly what the position is today is overstating their confidence.
The workable posture: build a library that needs no approval number because it makes no drug claim. Education, mechanism, tradition and honest evidence labelling sit outside the fight entirely.

callout.title: Your marketplace listings are advertising too
callout.body: The compliance conversation usually covers the website and stops there. Your Amazon and Flipkart listings, your Instagram captions and your affiliates' pages are advertising by the same definition. Audit them in the same pass, or you've cleaned one surface out of five.

sections.h2: Three clusters that carry the whole category
body: Ayurveda is unusually well suited to cluster-based SEO, because the domain already has a taxonomy. You don't need to invent an architecture. You need to stop publishing listicles instead of using the one that exists.

One page per herb, structured identically: Sanskrit and botanical name, part used, classical categorisation, traditional indications, preparation forms, research status, dosage as used in studies, contraindications. Ashwagandha, triphala, brahmi, guggulu, shatavari, giloy, neem, tulsi — each is standing demand that doesn't decay, and this is the cluster that earns links, because journalists and dietitians need something citable and there's little of it in English from Indian sources.

`vata pitta kapha meaning`, `how to know my body type`, `pitta diet chart` — enormous, evergreen, mostly served by foreign wellness blogs with a shaky grasp of the source material. An Indian brand with a vaidya on staff should own these and generally doesn't. A prakriti self-assessment tool is the one interactive asset here that reliably attracts links. Build it as a page, not a gated PDF.

Abhyanga, shirodhara, nasya, basti, virechana, the full panchakarma sequence. Write what happens minute by minute, what to wear, what the preparation days involve, how tired you'll be afterwards, what it costs. Sensory detail converts where benefit claims never will, and it sidesteps the claim problem completely.

bullets: Wire them together: the herb page links to the therapies it's used in, the therapy page back to the herbs, both to the relevant dosha page. That's a real [topic cluster](/glossary/topic-cluster), not a tag archive.
Product pages hang off the education, never the reverse. The monograph earns the ranking; the product link collects it.

sections.h2: Classical citation, and a vaidya with a name
body: Ayurvedic content has a self-inflicted authority problem. The tradition has primary texts — Charaka Samhita, Sushruta Samhita, Ashtanga Hridayam — and almost nobody cites them properly. The category publishes anonymous posts asserting benefits instead: no classical authority and no clinical evidence, the worst of both.

Do it the other way. Cite the text and chapter a traditional use comes from. Cite the trial, by name, where research exists. Where the two disagree, or nothing has been tested, say so in one plain sentence. That sentence is why a health journalist links to you.
bullets: **A named BAMS practitioner as author or reviewer**, with qualification and registration on a real bio page, and a review date. Undated health content reads as abandoned.
**Explicit labelling of claim type**: "traditionally indicated for" is a different sentence from "a randomised trial found", and readers can tell.

**No borrowed authority.** Don't cite a study on a purified extract at a dose your product doesn't contain. It's the category's commonest quiet fabrication and it collapses under one email from a journalist.

callout.title: Why this matters more after every core update
callout.body: Google's helpful-content and core updates have consistently hit anonymous, unsourced health content hardest, and ayurvedic sites were heavily represented in that pattern. Experience, expertise, authority and trust aren't a score you can buy. It's whether a reader can tell who wrote this and why they'd know.

sections.h2: Panchakarma centres and clinics: the local pages
body: Treatment centres are a second, separate SEO problem. `panchakarma centre near me`, `ayurvedic hospital in kochi`, `shirodhara in bangalore` are local-intent queries decided largely by proximity, profile completeness and reviews.

One Google Business Profile per centre, each linked to its own page — therapies at that address, the physicians who practise there, treatment durations, residential package details, real photographs. Kerala centres have a genuine seasonal spike: Karkidaka chikitsa, the monsoon-month treatment tradition, pulls a concentrated wave of searches every July and August. Publishing that page in June rather than July is the whole difference. Our [Kochi SEO page](/seo-agency/kochi) covers that market.
bullets: **NABH's AYUSH accreditation** is a trust signal almost nobody displays. If you hold it, put the number on the page.
**Residential packages** need day-by-day itineraries and total costs, not "starting from" teasers.
**Physician pages per centre** — international patients pick a doctor, not a building.

**No locality templates.** `ayurvedic centre in <every suburb>` pages for places you don't operate is thin content at scale, and it risks the whole domain rather than just those URLs. See [where programmatic SEO crosses the line](/journal/programmatic-seo-and-the-scaled-content-line).

sections.h2: The export search, and someone else's rulebook
body: Ayurvedic products and treatment centres both attract real overseas demand — the US, UK, Gulf, Europe, and the diaspora most of all. The searches differ from domestic ones: `authentic ayurvedic retreat kerala`, `ashwagandha supplement uk`, `is ayurveda safe`, `ayurvedic treatment cost india`.

The trap is assuming your Indian pages can serve them. Legally they can't. US supplement marketing runs on structure-function claims with a mandatory disclaimer stating the claim hasn't been evaluated by the FDA and the product isn't intended to diagnose, treat, cure or prevent disease. In the EU only authorised health claims under Regulation (EC) 1924/2006 may be used, and most botanical claims sit in a long-running "on hold" limbo. A claim that's merely risky here is non-compliant in both.
bullets: **Separate the market pages** and implement `hreflang` properly, with claim language written per market rather than translated.

**Publish your testing.** Importing markets scrutinise heavy metals in traditional medicines and recalls are public. A certificate-of-analysis page with batch results is a trust asset, and it ranks for the safety queries your competitors pretend nobody types.

**Price in the reader's currency** with a stated conversion date, flag shipping restrictions before checkout, and give centre enquiries a visa and travel page covering documents, treatment length and whether family can stay.

sections.h2: What it costs, and what we actually guarantee
body: An ayurvedic brand with a catalogue, a herb and therapy library and a compliance review loop sits at ₹75,000/mo with us. A single clinic or centre starts at ₹40,000/mo. Export work adds scope, because it's a separate content set per market rather than a translation. All ex-GST, month-to-month after the first quarter, every asset yours — see [pricing](/pricing).

The cost that surprises people isn't the writing. It's the vaidya's review time, and the discipline to cut the sentence that would have sold better. We don't promise a ranking position. Nobody controls Google's index, and a category this badly served by exaggerated promises shouldn't buy another. We freeze your trailing-90-day qualified organic leads on day one and beat that number within 90 days, or we keep working free until we do. That's why we take three clients a month.

callout.title: What to expect, and when
callout.body: Herb and therapy clusters take four to six months to compound — they need internal linking and citations to mature, and the competition includes established international wellness publishers. Clinic listings move faster, often four to eight weeks. Export markets are slowest: you're a new domain in another country's results.

faqs.q: What can't an ayurvedic brand say in its marketing in India?
faqs.a: You cannot advertise a remedy as preventing or curing the conditions listed under the Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954 and Schedule J of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules — diabetes, obesity, cancer, hypertension and many more. Education, traditional use and honestly labelled research are all fine.

faqs.q: Is Rule 170 still in force for Ayush advertising?
faqs.a: Its status has genuinely moved several times — notification, advisories against enforcement, a proposal to omit it, and Supreme Court scrutiny of misleading Ayush advertising. Anyone stating a flat answer is guessing. Build content that makes no drug claim, and the question stops mattering to your marketing.

faqs.q: What content actually ranks for ayurvedic brands?
faqs.a: Three clusters carry the category: herb monographs with botanical names, traditional use and research status; dosha and prakriti explainers; and therapy pages describing what actually happens during abhyanga, shirodhara or a panchakarma sequence. Product pages hang off that education rather than replacing it.

faqs.q: Do we need a BAMS doctor to write our content?
faqs.a: To write it, not necessarily. To review and sign it, yes. Health content is judged on demonstrated expertise, and a named practitioner with a registration number is the cheapest credibility available to you. It's also what stops a well-meaning writer from publishing a claim that breaches the DMR Act.

faqs.q: Can we use our Indian product pages for US and UK customers?
faqs.a: No. US supplement marketing runs on structure-function claims with a mandatory FDA disclaimer, and the EU permits only authorised health claims under Regulation 1924/2006, with most botanical claims still on hold. Write the claim language per market and separate the pages with hreflang.

faqs.q: How long does SEO take for an ayurvedic ecommerce site?
faqs.a: Four to six months for herb and therapy clusters to compound, because they need internal links and citations to mature and you're competing with established international wellness publishers. Branded product searches move earlier. Clinic and centre listings are the fastest, often four to eight weeks.
